title: latency-attribution-census-p50p95p99
body:
Summary:

This doc summarizes an end-to-end latency "census" across our primary inference path (hosted API -> router -> runtime -> GPU execution -> return). The goal: produce an attribution breakdown for p50/p95/p99 across common request archetypes and identify small-scope remediation candidates that give the best SLO ROI. This is a working note with raw numbers, sampling methodology, outlier heuristics, and proposed follow-ups.

Motivation / context:
- Recent customer reports and SLO alerts show p95 regressions on mid-size models for sequence lengths >= 512.
- Previous microbenchmarks indicate kernel-level performance is within expected ranges, but customer-visible latency still high in tail.
- Need an operationally-actionable breakdown (percent and absolute ms) per stage so we can prioritize fixes for dedicated vs hosted routing.

Test matrix (what we measured):
- Models: redwood-7b-v2 (FP16), redwood-13b-v1 (Q4), redwood-70b-moderate (FP16, sampled).
- Sequence lengths: 64, 256, 512, 1024 (tokens).
- Workloads: single-turn text generation (streaming enabled), batched generation (batch size 4), multi-session chat (prefix reuse).
- Regions/hardware: us-west-2 (A100-80GB), us-east-1 (H100-80GB), dedicated pool (mixed V100 legacy).
- Sample size: 10k requests per cell (stratified over request arrival times). Traces collected via X-trace header + per-hop spans.

Instrumentation and heuristics:
- Stage boundaries: ingress (HTTP accept + TLS), load-balancer -> router handoff, routing policy evaluation, request serialization, model selection/lookup, tokenization, runtime scheduling (enqueue to GPU), GPU execution (per-token compute), KV cache lookup, post-processing (detokenize + formatting), response flush/streaming overhead, and egress (network).
- Clock sync: root timestamps are host-monotonic; cross-node correlation uses trace ID with max skew correction. We discard traces where skew > 15ms for p99 analysis (about 0.8% of samples).
- Outliers: For p99 we keep top 1% but tag spikes caused by infra maintenance windows and remove them from the baseline summary.

High-level results (aggregated):
- p50 overall: 52 ms (seq=64), 88 ms (seq=256), 150 ms (seq=512), 320 ms (seq=1024)
- p95 overall: 120 ms (seq=64), 230 ms (seq=256), 520 ms (seq=512), 1,200 ms (seq=1024)
- p99 overall: 320 ms (seq=64), 610 ms (seq=256), 1,850 ms (seq=512), 6,400 ms (seq=1024)

Stage attribution examples (redwood-13b-v1, seq=512, single-turn, streaming disabled):
- Network ingress (TLS accept + LB): p50 8ms, p95 20ms, p99 55ms
- Router policy eval + model lookup: p50 4ms, p95 12ms, p99 40ms
- Request serialization & proto marshal: p50 3ms, p95 8ms, p99 25ms
- Tokenization: p50 12ms, p95 30ms, p99 80ms
- Runtime scheduling (enqueue + queue wait): p50 14ms, p95 90ms, p99 700ms
- GPU execution (compute + per-token kernel): p50 42ms, p95 260ms, p99 1,200ms
- KV cache lookup (miss-heavy prefix): p50 5ms, p95 18ms, p99 120ms
- Post-process (detokenize + format): p50 3ms, p95 10ms, p99 30ms
- Streaming flush/egress: p50 7ms, p95 12ms, p99 35ms

Notes on the above attribution:
- The scheduling queue dominates the tail (p99) compared to compute for this workload. Many p99 traces show long wait times in the runtime scheduler prior to reaching GPU.
- For p95, both GPU compute and scheduling are significant; for p50 the GPU compute is the largest single contributor.
- Tokenization is non-negligible and more variable for long sequences because we run single-threaded tokenizers in the request path for safety (we conservatively avoid shared tokenizer libs on multi-tenant hosts).

Comparative snapshots (seq=256, batch=4, redwood-7b-v2 on A100):
- p50: 46ms overall. Stage shares: scheduling 20%, compute 35%, networking 10%, tokenization 12%, other 23%
- p95: 210ms overall. Stage shares: scheduling 30%, compute 45%, networking 8%, tokenization 6%, other 11%
- p99: 580ms overall. Stage shares: scheduling 40%, compute 35%, networking 6%, tokenization 4%, other 15%

Key root causes found in traces:
1) Runtime scheduler hot spots: when concurrency is high, our scheduler's fairness policy degenerates and tasks block waiting for a GPU slot. Evidence: long enqueue-to-start gaps correlated with certain host CPU load patterns and GC pauses in the runtime process.
2) Tokenizer latency spikes: single-threaded tokenizer calls within request handling cause head-of-line blocking at tails when GC or CPU steal occurs.
3) Network variance correlated with TLS renegotiation backoffs on older LB instances; contributes a few hundred ms to p99 occasionally.
4) KV-cache eviction storms: when many different sessions touch cold prefixes, we observe higher KV lookup latency and backend IOPS saturation that pushes up p99 for prefix-heavy workloads.

Small-scope remediation candidates (ranked by expected latency tail reduction per engineer-day):
- Fix A: Scheduler yield and preemption tweaks (estimated 2 engineer-days) -> expect 30–45% reduction in scheduling p99 waits.
- Fix B: Move tokenizer to a shared, warmed microservice (3 engineer-days + infra) -> lower tokenization p99 by ~60% and remove head-of-line blocking. Risk: additional network hop; mitigations: persistent connection pooling + local hot-cache.
- Fix C: Tune LB TLS session reuse and upgrade older LB fleet (1.5 engineer-days ops) -> reduce sporadic network p99 spikes.
- Fix D: Throttle aggressive prefix writes + background async warmup for KV cache (4 engineer-days) -> reduce KV lookup tail, especially for multi-session churn workloads.

Experiments run (short notes):
- Scheduler A/B: enabled preemption heuristics on a 10% slice of traffic for 3 days. Outcome: p95 improved by 18% and p99 improved by 26% on that slice. No increase in error rates.
- Tokenizer offload: proof-of-concept moved tokenization to a local sidecar process on half of hosts. Outcome: tokenization p99 decreased 52% but overall p99 unaffected until scheduler fix deployed (tokens were not the dominant tail in that workload).

Operational recommendations (near-term):
- Ship scheduler preemption tweaks to canary (target week 2). Monitor: latency p95/p99, GPU utilization, scheduling fairness metrics.
- Deploy LB TLS session reuse changes with canary policy. Prioritize older LB instances in us-east-1.
- Start design for tokenizer sidecar as an opt-in feature for heavy-prefix tenants. Evaluate cost vs latency tradeoffs.

Longer-term work and tradeoffs:
- Re-architect runtime queue: shift from centralized fair-queue to per-tenant token bucket with opportunistic packing. Benefit: reduces cross-tenant head-of-line blocking. Cost: medium (6–8 engineer-weeks) and requires rollout coordination with Dedicated customers.
- Kernel-level optimizations: further fuse attention kernels for >1k sequences. Benefit mainly for large-seq p50/p95; cost: ML-research + infra testing.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of scheduler p99 is due to noisy neighbors vs GC/host-level interference? We need machine-level jvm/containers traces aligned with latency traces for deeper attribution.
- For the tokenizer service approach: will added network hop re-introduce tail at cluster-level under load? Need load tests with realistic multi-tenant churn.
- Is KV backend the right abstraction for prefix caching under multi-tenant conditions, or do we need a local LRU with async refill?

Action items (owners):
- Asha: finalize scheduler preemption patch and open PR (github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/456) - due 2025-01-20
- Marco: run host-level telemetry collection for 7 days on canary fleet (cpu/gc/interrupts) and attach traces (JIRA-RT-872) - due 2025-01-24
- Sophie: prototype tokenizer sidecar and perf harness (POC repo link in Confluence-1234) - due 2025-02-07
- Ethan: LB fleet audit and TLS reuse rollout plan with infra (ticket created) - due 2025-01-18

Appendix A: sampling methodology (short)
- Traces were sampled uniformly over 72-hour windows to capture diurnal patterns. We used deterministic sampling keyed by customer_id to ensure repeatability.
- For p99 we used stratified sampling + retention of top 2% across windows to ensure we did not miss bursty infra events.

Appendix B: example raw trace (single p99 event) - redwood-13b-v1 seq=512
- ingress 12ms -> router 9ms -> serialize 4ms -> tokenize 18ms -> enqueue 12ms -> queue-wait 1,120ms -> gpu-start -> gpu-compute 540ms -> kv-lookup 62ms -> post 10ms -> flush 8ms -> egress 9ms
- Notes: queue-wait spike correlated with host CPU steal + concurrent large-batch job on same host.

Appendix C: monitoring signals to add
- scheduler.queue_wait_histogram (per-model, per-host)
- tokenizer.latency.{p50,p95,p99} (per-tenant)
- kv.backend_iops and cache_fill_rate
- lb.tls_renegotiations_count (per-lb-instance)

Comments welcome. If we agree on near-term fixes, I will convert this into a formal RFC with rollout and rollback plans.
